exercises.prompt: Implement checked_sqrt(x) so it returns the square root of x (as a float) — but raises ValueError when x is negative, since a real square root is undefined there. checked_sqrt(9) is 3.0 and checked_sqrt(0) is 0.0, while checked_sqrt(-1) raises ValueError. Guard the bad case first, then return x ** 0.5 for any x that is 0 or greater.
hints: Test the invalid case at the top: if x is negative there is no answer to return, so raise instead of computing.
raise ValueError('...') stops the function and signals the bad input; put it behind an if x < 0 guard, then return the root below.
if x < 0: raise ValueError('x must be non-negative'), then return x ** 0.5 — the guard is < (not <=), so checked_sqrt(0) still returns 0.0 while a negative input raises.

exercises.prompt: Implement safe_divide(a, b) so it returns a / b, but raises ZeroDivisionError when b is 0 rather than letting the division fail silently or return something misleading. safe_divide(10, 2) is 5.0 and safe_divide(7, 2) is 3.5, while safe_divide(1, 0) raises ZeroDivisionError. A zero numerator is fine: safe_divide(0, 5) is 0.0.
hints: The one input to reject is a divisor of 0 — guard it before you divide, since that is the only value of b with no valid result.
if b == 0: raise ZeroDivisionError('...'), then return a / b for every other divisor.
Use true division a / b (not //): it returns a float, so safe_divide(7, 2) is 3.5, and the guard means only b == 0 raises — a zero numerator like safe_divide(0, 5) is a perfectly fine 0.0.

exercises.prompt: Implement get_at(xs, i) so it returns the element of the list xs at index i, but raises IndexError when i is out of range — that is, when i is negative or i is greater than or equal to len(xs). get_at([10, 20, 30], 0) is 10 and get_at([10, 20, 30], 2) is 30, while get_at([10, 20, 30], 3) and get_at([10, 20, 30], -1) both raise IndexError. An empty list raises IndexError for any i.
hints: A valid index runs from 0 up to len(xs) − 1; anything outside that — negative, or too big — has no element to return.
Guard with if i < 0 or i >= len(xs): raise IndexError('...'), then return xs[i] when i is in range.
You must check i < 0 yourself: a plain return xs[i] would let xs[-1] succeed and return the last element, so the get_at(..., -1) test is what forces the explicit lower-bound guard.

exercises.prompt: Implement parse_positive(n) so it returns n unchanged when n is a positive number, but raises ValueError when n is zero or negative. parse_positive(5) is 5 and parse_positive(1) is 1, while parse_positive(0) and parse_positive(-3) both raise ValueError. The boundary matters: 0 is NOT positive, so it raises.
hints: Only strictly positive numbers are allowed through — so 0, like any negative, must be rejected.
if n <= 0: raise ValueError('...'), then return n for anything larger.
The guard is <= (not <), so parse_positive(0) raises while parse_positive(1) returns 1 — putting the boundary exactly at 0.

exercises.prompt: Implement require_int(x) so it returns x unchanged when x is an int, but raises TypeError when x is any other type — a str, a float, a list, and so on. require_int(5) is 5, while require_int('5') and require_int(3.0) both raise TypeError. Use isinstance(x, int) to test the type; do NOT convert the value, just accept or reject it.
hints: This guard is about the type of the value, not its size — the wrong KIND of value is what you reject.
isinstance(x, int) is True only for integers; raise TypeError when it is not, then return x.
if not isinstance(x, int): raise TypeError('expected an int'), then return x — note require_int('5') must raise rather than convert, and require_int(3.0) raises too because a float is not an int.
